title: Why Clean and Soiled Linen Should Be Kept Separate
excerpt: Clean and soiled linen should be separated because laundering removes contamination, but later contact with dirty textiles, carts, surfaces or handling can contaminate clean items again.
content_html:
Separating clean and soiled linen protects the work already achieved by laundering. Once a textile has been cleaned, any unnecessary contact with dirty items or dirty-side equipment creates a new opportunity for contamination.

The dirty side has a different risk

Soiled textiles may carry body soil, dust, fluids and microorganisms. CDC recommends containing soiled linen and keeping dirty-linen handling within a controlled workflow.

The clean side is a protection zone

Clean linen no longer needs soil-removal handling. It needs protection from dust, debris, soiled textiles, dirty carts and contaminated work surfaces during folding, storage and transport.

Physical separation reduces cross-contact

CDC guidance recommends separation between soiled-linen processing and clean-linen storage. Where possible, workflow should move from dirty to clean without clean items travelling back through the dirty side.

Carts and containers matter

A clean textile can be recontaminated by a dirty cart or container. Dedicated or appropriately cleaned transport equipment helps preserve clean status after laundering.

Hands and surfaces can bridge the two sides

Staff movement, gloves, hands and worktables can transfer contamination if clean and dirty tasks are mixed. Procedures should define when hand hygiene, PPE changes and surface cleaning are required.

Storage completes the separation

Clean linen should be stored in a designated clean area and protected from splash, dust and contact with soiled items. Good separation continues until the textile is actually issued for use.

Practical takeaway

Clean/dirty separation prevents recontamination. The control applies to rooms, carts, containers, surfaces, staff movement and storage—not just to two piles of laundry.

References

  1. CDC — Appendix D: Linen and Laundry Management.
  2. CDC — Laundry and Bedding.
  3. CDC — Textiles and Laundry.
